CoSPlay: Cooperative Self-Play at Test-Time with Self-Generated Code and Unit Test

Zhangyi Hu Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)    Chenhui Liu Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)    Tian Huang Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)    Jindong Li Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)    Yang Yang Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)    Jiemin Wu Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)    Zining Zhong Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)    Menglin Yang Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)    Yutao Yue Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou) Affiliation: Institute of Deep Perception Technology, JITRI, Wuxi, China Github Page Dataset & Log * 2026-5-13

1 Introduction

Recently, advanced by RLVR [6, 40, 33] and TTS [3, 20, 23], LLMs have achieved significant progress in coding capability. In code generation, UTs provide executable input-output checks that make functional correctness verifiable [35, 41]. This has made them widely used for guiding recent code-generation methods. As shown in Figure 2, SOTA RLVR methods leverage large collections of GT UTs for training, i.e. test cases with guaranteed-correct input-output pairs, typically curated by human experts or official problem setters [22, 44, 35]. However, curating such GT UTs is too costly to scale [4, 21], and GT-free RLVR methods like Absolute-Zero [47] still remain less competitive in practice and require costly model-weight updates [42, 48].

While TTS methods avoid weight updates, they still need to evaluate the code quality at inference time for refinement, filtering, and selection. When GT UTs are available, these decisions can be grounded in trusted input-output checks [16, 28, 41, 49]. In GT-free settings, however, it must be constructed from self-generated UTs, typically by sampling codes and tests before heuristic or mathematical re-ranking [4, 9]; we provide a broader discussion in Appendix C. Yet scaling this pipeline is fragile: generated UTs may have incorrect expected outputs, fail to distinguish among plausible candidates, or spuriously agree with wrong code [38]. The key question therefore shifts from merely sampling more code or UTs to a co-evolution perspective: Can codes and UTs co-evolve at inference time to achieve competitive code generation without GT?

To this end, we present CoSPlay, a GT-free, training-free three-stage pipeline that creates a co-evolving loop between code candidates and UTs. First, Exploration-Attack-Guided Code-UT Idea Generation bootstraps the loop by exploring plausible solution strategies and deriving targeted UT ideas from their potential failure modes, so the initial UT pool is grounded in solution-specific assumptions and can better distinguish plausible code candidates. Given this initialized pool, Execution-Matrix-Driven Iterative Self-Play lets codes and UTs evaluate each other: high-support UTs provide reliable refinement signals, while high-support codes provide evidence for judging UTs. These pass-count signals guide code-side pruning/refinement and UT-side refreshing/replacement, progressively improving both pools. Finally, when the evolved Code-UT pool still leaves BoN-tied codes, Output-Consensus-Based Cluster Selection handles the remaining ambiguity among BoN-tied codes by comparing their outputs on random valid inputs and selecting the most reliable consensus cluster and code, since correct codes should agree while incorrect codes tend to diverge.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  1. 1.

    We introduce CoSPlay, a GT-free, training-free framework that enables code candidates and self-generated UT to co-evolve at test-time, providing a scalable inference strategy for competitive code generation without any GT-data.

  2. 2.

    Extensive experiments across four challenging coding benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness, generalizability, and scalability of CoSPlay. It matches or surpasses strong RLVR models trained with massive GT UTs and improves various BoN across instruct, RLVR-tuned, and frontier-scale backbones. Under comparable output-token budgets, CoSPlay outperforms existing GT-free TTS methods, and its performance continues to rise as the budget is scaled up.

  3. 3.

    We establish internal quality-evaluation principles for GT-free Code-UT co-evolution. Without GT labels, UT pass counts estimate test reliability, code pass counts estimate code candidate quality, and output-consensus clusters estimate final-selection confidence. Theory and before/after self-play studies show that these signals correlate with true quality and reliably support co-evolution, offering practical diagnostics for future GT-free code generation methods.

2 Methodology

2.1 Exploration-Attack-Guided Code and UT Idea Generation

Directly prompting the LLM to generate UTs often yields generic or superficial cases, because the tests are not grounded in the way code candidates may fail [2]. Discriminative UTs instead target solution-specific assumptions: for example, duplicate elements can expose solutions that incorrectly assume all values are unique. Motivated by PlanSearch [34], we therefore explore plausible solution strategies in natural language and derive corresponding targeted UT ideas from their potential failure modes. Let 𝒫\mathcal{P} denote the problem description. The exploration proceeds in two steps: (i) Solution exploration. We first prompt the LLM to produce a set of high-level algorithmic hints ℋ={hi}i=1n\mathcal{H}=\{h_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}, covering likely strategies, data structures, and edge cases implied by 𝒫\mathcal{P}. These hints are not intended to be complete solutions, but to span diverse solution directions. We then construct a subset space Ω={ω⊆ℋ∣|ω|∈{1,2}}\Omega=\{\omega\subseteq\mathcal{H}\mid|\omega|\in\{1,2\}\} and prompt the LLM to expand each hint subset ω∈Ω\omega\in\Omega into a set of detailed natural-language solution plans 𝒮ω\mathcal{S}_{\omega}, yielding the solution-plan pool 𝒮=⋃ω∈Ω𝒮ω\mathcal{S}=\bigcup_{\omega\in\Omega}\mathcal{S}_{\omega}. Limiting the subset size to 1 or 2 balances solution diversity against combinatorial explosion. (ii) Failure-oriented UT attack idea exploration. For each plan s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S}, we ask the LLM to identify potential failure modes, hidden edge cases, and implementation pitfalls. This yields a UT attack idea set 𝒜s\mathcal{A}_{s}, and we define the final UT attack idea pool as 𝒜=⋃s∈𝒮𝒜s\mathcal{A}=\bigcup_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\mathcal{A}_{s}.

2.2 Code and UT Initialization

Pool Construction. Starting from the solution-plan pool 𝒮\mathcal{S} and the UT attack-idea pool 𝒜\mathcal{A}, we build the initial code and UT pools for self-play. For the code pool 𝒞={ci}i=1Nc\mathcal{C}=\{c_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N_{c}}, we shuffle 𝒮\mathcal{S} and use each selected plan once to prompt the LLM for one candidate cic_{i}. For the UT pool 𝒯={tj}j=1Nt\mathcal{T}=\{t_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N_{t}}, candidate inputs come from two sources. The random source asks the LLM to produce a valid input directly from the problem statement. The attack source shuffles 𝒜\mathcal{A} and asks the LLM to instantiate each selected idea as a concrete valid input. For each input xjx_{j}, we ask the LLM to solve it multiple times; if the sampled outputs mostly agree, we take the agreed answer as yjy_{j} and add tj=(xj,yj)t_{j}=(x_{j},y_{j}) to 𝒯\mathcal{T}.

Intuition of UT Sampling Strategy. To start self-play and co-evolve the two pools, we need an advantage signal that can judge the quality of generated samples. Specifically, correct code should be more likely to pass generated UTs than wrong code, and correct UTs should be more likely to be passed by generated code than wrong-output UTs. Appendix A.1.1 derives the quality threshold required for each advantage to hold, with a looser code quality threshold for judging UTs and a stricter UT quality threshold for judging code. To meet this stricter UT quality requirement, we apply output self-consistency: a candidate input is kept only when multiple sampled outputs agree on the same answer, which raises the correctness prior of the initial UT pool. However, this filter is uneven across sources. Attack-derived inputs from 𝒜\mathcal{A} are highly discriminative because they target plausible failure modes, but their expected outputs are also harder for the LLM to infer [26], so self-consistency may discard some otherwise useful probes before self-play begins. We therefore supplement the pool with random valid inputs sampled directly from the problem statement, which provide broader sanity checks under the same self-consistency criterion.

2.3 Execution-Matrix-Driven Iterative Self-Play

Setup. Given the execution matrix 𝐌∈{0,1}Nc×Nt\mathbf{M}\in\{0,1\}^{N_{c}\times N_{t}}, where 𝐌i​j=1\mathbf{M}_{ij}=1 indicates that code cic_{i} passes UT tjt_{j}, we define the UT pass count pjUTp^{\mathrm{UT}}_{j} as the number of code candidates that pass UT tjt_{j}, and the code pass count picodep^{\mathrm{code}}_{i} as the number of UTs passed by code candidate cic_{i}. We also define their normalized pass rates αjUT\alpha^{\mathrm{UT}}_{j} and αicode\alpha^{\mathrm{code}}_{i}:

pjUT=∑i=1Nc𝐌i​j,picode=∑j=1Nt𝐌i​j,αjUT=pjUT/Nc,αicode=picode/Nt,p^{\mathrm{UT}}_{j}=\sum_{i=1}^{N_{c}}\mathbf{M}_{ij},\quad p^{\mathrm{code}}_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{N_{t}}\mathbf{M}_{ij},\quad\alpha^{\mathrm{UT}}_{j}=p^{\mathrm{UT}}_{j}/{N_{c}},\quad\alpha^{\mathrm{code}}_{i}=p^{\mathrm{code}}_{i}/N_{t}, (1)

Pass-count Signal. The initial codes/UTs are produced by independent sampling. For ease of analysis, we therefore follow prior work that analyzes pass-count-based signals under idealized i.i.d. assumptions [4, 9, 24, 35]. Theorem A.1 shows that, when the advantage thresholds in Eq. 10 hold, i.e., correct codes are more likely to pass generated UTs and correct UTs are more likely to be passed by generated codes, both sides have a positive posterior direction: higher code/UT pass counts imply a larger posterior probability of correctness. Our empirical results in Figure 4 further support this correlation in realistic Round-0 settings before self-play: correct codes/UTs concentrate more in high-pass-count regions, and their GT correctness increases with pass count. Thus, we use pass counts to guide execution-matrix diagnosis.

Self-play Pipeline. Each play iteration alternates over four steps: pruning all-failing codes, refreshing lowest-support non-trivial UTs to break spurious Code-UT coupling, refining codes with highest-support non-trivial UTs, and replacing zero-discrimination UTs. After each step, we re-execute all Code-UT pairs to refresh 𝐌\mathbf{M}, since updating one pool can change the diagnostic status of the other. A step is skipped if no target code/UT exists, and the loop terminates when all entries of 𝐌\mathbf{M} become 11 or the iteration budget TmaxT_{\max} is reached.

Step ①: Code Cleaning. All-failing codes and zero-support UTs carry different information. If each validated UT has probability ρT>0\rho_{T}>0 of having the correct output, then a code with αicode=0\alpha^{\mathrm{code}}_{i}=0 fails at least one correct UT with probability 1−(1−ρT)Nt1-(1-\rho_{T})^{N_{t}}, which approaches one exponentially in NtN_{t}. Output self-consistency raises this UT prior, making the judgment more reliable. Such code is therefore likely incorrect and provides little signal for improving the UT pool [32]. By contrast, a zero-support UT may still be a valid hard probe that exposes a shared bug in the current code pool, so deleting it may discard useful tests. We therefore first remove all-failing codes and replace them with newly generated ones:

𝒞←(𝒞∖𝒞fail)∪𝒞new,\mathcal{C}\leftarrow(\mathcal{C}\setminus\mathcal{C}_{\text{fail}})\cup\mathcal{C}_{\text{new}}, (2)

where 𝒞fail={ci∈𝒞|αicode=0}\mathcal{C}_{\text{fail}}=\{c_{i}\in\mathcal{C}\mathrel{|}\alpha^{\mathrm{code}}_{i}=0\}, and 𝒞new\mathcal{C}_{\text{new}} denotes new codes given a solution idea from 𝒮\mathcal{S}, with |𝒞new|=|𝒞fail||\mathcal{C}_{\text{new}}|=|\mathcal{C}_{\text{fail}}|.

Step ②: Breaking Spurious Code-UT Coupling. After code cleaning, we turn to diagnose the UT pool before using it for refinement. A UT with a low but non-zero pass rate (i.e. non-trivial worst) is risky: unlike a zero-pass UT, which rejects all codes universally, it is supported by only a small subset of codes and may therefore reflect spurious coupling with a specific wrong logic. If such a UT is chosen for code refinement, it can propagate the minority behavior to other codes. The goal is not to discard low-support UTs indiscriminately, but to break the suspicious agreement between a minority code behavior and a potentially coupled UT. We therefore refresh this UT by providing the LLM with the original UT and the code it spuriously passed, instructing it to generate a new UT given 𝒜\mathcal{A} while avoiding the same suspicious agreement pattern.

𝒯←(𝒯∖𝒯jworst)∪𝒯jworst′,\mathcal{T}\leftarrow(\mathcal{T}\setminus\mathcal{T}_{j_{\mathrm{worst}}})\cup\mathcal{T}^{\prime}_{j_{\mathrm{worst}}}, (3)

where jworst=arg⁡minj​{αjUT∣0<αjUT<1}j_{\mathrm{worst}}=\arg\min_{j}\{\alpha^{{\mathrm{UT}}}_{j}\mid 0<\alpha^{{\mathrm{UT}}}_{j}<1\} denotes the selected UT index, 𝒯jworst\mathcal{T}_{j_{\mathrm{worst}}} is the original UT, and 𝒯jworst′\mathcal{T}^{\prime}_{j_{\mathrm{worst}}} is the regenerated UT given an attack idea from 𝒜\mathcal{A} with 𝒯jworst\mathcal{T}_{j_{\mathrm{worst}}} and its passed codes. We do not assume the selected UT is necessarily wrong; it serves as a practical proxy for the UT most likely to be spuriously coupled.

Step ③: Code Fixing. After code cleaning and replacing the most suspicious UT, we turn to refine buggy codes using a trustworthy yet discriminative UT. A UT with αjUT=1\alpha^{{\mathrm{UT}}}_{j}=1 may be trustworthy enough but provides no refinement signal. We therefore select the UT with the highest pass rate but strictly below 11, i.e., the non-trivial best UT which is reliable enough and can still distinguish buggy codes. For each code failing this UT, we provide the LLM with the buggy code, the UT itself, and the actual output of the code to guide refinement:

𝒞←(𝒞∖𝒞target)∪𝒞fixed,\mathcal{C}\leftarrow(\mathcal{C}\setminus\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{target}})\cup\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{fixed}}, (4)

where jbest=arg⁡maxj​{αjUT∣0<αjUT<1}j_{\mathrm{best}}=\arg\max_{j}\{\alpha^{\mathrm{UT}}_{j}\mid 0<\alpha^{\mathrm{UT}}_{j}<1\} denotes the index of selected high-support yet non-trivial UT. 𝒞target={ci∈𝒞∣𝐌i,jbest=0}\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{target}}=\{c_{i}\in\mathcal{C}\mid\mathbf{M}_{i,j_{\mathrm{best}}}=0\} denotes the code candidates that fail the selected UT tjbestt_{j_{\mathrm{best}}} and are therefore targeted for refinement. 𝒞fixed\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{fixed}} denotes the refined versions of 𝒞target\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{target}}, generated using tjbestt_{j_{\mathrm{best}}} and the corresponding execution feedback.

Step ④: Replacing Zero-Discrimination UTs. Because code refinement improves the code pool, previously discriminative UTs may become trivial under the updated pool: they are either passed by all candidates (αjUT=1\alpha^{{\mathrm{UT}}}_{j}=1) or by none (αjUT=0\alpha^{{\mathrm{UT}}}_{j}=0). All-pass UTs are too easy for the current code pool, whereas a zero-pass-rate UT is more likely to be noisy or mismatched to the current code pool [31, 38]. Since such UTs no longer provide useful refinement or selection signals [8, 24], we replace them with newly generated UTs from 𝒜\mathcal{A}:

𝒯←(𝒯∖𝒯triv)∪𝒯new,\mathcal{T}\leftarrow(\mathcal{T}\setminus\mathcal{T}_{\text{triv}})\cup\mathcal{T}_{\text{new}}, (5)

where 𝒯triv={(xj,yj)∈𝒯∣αjUT∈{0,1}}\mathcal{T}_{\text{triv}}=\{(x_{j},y_{j})\in\mathcal{T}\mid\alpha^{{\mathrm{UT}}}_{j}\in\{0,1\}\} denotes the set of zero-discrimination UTs, and 𝒯new\mathcal{T}_{\text{new}} is the set of newly generated UTs. We maintain a constant UT pool size by enforcing |𝒯new|=|𝒯triv||\mathcal{T}_{\text{new}}|=|\mathcal{T}_{\text{triv}}|.

2.4 Output-Consensus-Based Cluster Selection

After self-play, we score each code by its final pass count picodep_{i}^{\mathrm{code}} and retain the BoN-tied top subset 𝒞high={ci∈𝒞∣picode=maxℓ⁡pℓcode}.\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{high}}=\left\{c_{i}\in\mathcal{C}\mid p_{i}^{\mathrm{code}}=\max_{\ell}p_{\ell}^{\mathrm{code}}\right\}. Because discrete pass counts can leave multiple top-scoring candidates, BoN alone cannot break ties. We thus apply an unsupervised execution-consensus clustering: we prompt the LLM to generate RR random and valid inputs 𝒵={zr}r=1R\mathcal{Z}=\{z_{r}\}_{r=1}^{R} which do not require outputs, and each ci∈𝒞highc_{i}\in\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{high}} is executed on 𝒵\mathcal{Z}. With oi​(zr)o_{i}(z_{r}) denoting the observed output of cic_{i} on zrz_{r}, each code induces the output signature σ⁡(ci):=(oi​(z1),…,oi​(zR))\sigma(c_{i}):=(o_{i}(z_{1}),\ldots,o_{i}(z_{R})).

Theoretical Motivation. Correct code candidates should share the same output signature, while incorrect code candidates typically split across different behaviors. As the number of random inputs increases, matching any fixed wrong signature becomes exponentially harder, whereas all correct candidates keep sharing the true signature. Thus, the true signature becomes the dominant population mode, and the empirical largest-cluster rule converges to it as the independently sampled candidate pool grows. Proposition A.3 formalizes this statement, with the proof given in Appendix A.

Clustering with Execution Errors. In practice, some executions may fail to produce a normal output, we mark these cases as oi​(zr)=ERRo_{i}(z_{r})=\mathrm{ERR}. We first define a pairwise observed-compatibility relation between codes. Two candidates ci,cj∈𝒞highc_{i},c_{j}\in\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{high}} are observed-compatible, denoted ci∼obscjc_{i}\sim_{\mathrm{obs}}c_{j}, if they produce the same valid output on every random input:

ci∼obscj⇔oi(zr)=oj(zr),∀r∈{1,…,R}:oi(zr)≠ERR∧oj(zr)≠ERR.c_{i}\sim_{\mathrm{obs}}c_{j}\iff o_{i}(z_{r})=o_{j}(z_{r}),\quad\forall r\in\{1,\ldots,R\}:\ o_{i}(z_{r})\neq\mathrm{ERR}\wedge\ o_{j}(z_{r})\neq\mathrm{ERR}. (6)

Execution errors are treated as missing evidence rather than output conflicts. Then we build output-consensus clusters over 𝒞high\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{high}}. Let 𝒢={Gm}m=1M\mathcal{G}=\{G_{m}\}_{m=1}^{M} denote the resulting collection, where MM is the number of clusters produced and each Gm⊆𝒞highG_{m}\subseteq\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{high}} contains code candidates with no observed output conflict. Because this compatibility relation may not be transitive when ERR\mathrm{ERR} are ignored, it does not directly induce a unique partition. We therefore construct conservative pairwise-compatible clusters by processing candidates in a fixed deterministic order. Specifically, when processing a candidate cic_{i}, we add it to an existing cluster GmG_{m} only if it is compatible with every member of that cluster, i.e. ∀cj∈Gm,ci∼obscj.\forall c_{j}\in G_{m},\ c_{i}\sim_{\mathrm{obs}}c_{j}. If no such cluster exists, cic_{i} starts a new cluster.

Reliability Scoring and Selection. In the error-free case, selecting the largest cluster is sufficient. With runtime errors, however, candidates with many failed executions may appear compatible due to few valid comparisons. We therefore score clusters by ordered valid pairwise agreements. For ci,cj∈Gmc_{i},c_{j}\in G_{m} and input zkz_{k}, define

ai​j(k)={oi​(zk)≠ERR,oj​(zk)≠ERR,oi​(zk)=oj​(zk)}.a_{ij}^{(k)}=\mathbf{1}\!\left\{o_{i}(z_{k})\neq\mathrm{ERR},\ o_{j}(z_{k})\neq\mathrm{ERR},\ o_{i}(z_{k})=o_{j}(z_{k})\right\}. (7)

We define the individual reliability score Sind​(ci)S_{\mathrm{ind}}(c_{i}) and the cluster reliability score Scls​(Gm)S_{\mathrm{cls}}(G_{m}) as

Sind​(ci)=∑cj∈Gm∖{ci}∑k=1Rai​j(k),Scls​(Gm)=∑ci∈GmSind​(ci).S_{\mathrm{ind}}(c_{i})=\sum_{c_{j}\in G_{m}\setminus\{c_{i}\}}\sum_{k=1}^{R}a_{ij}^{(k)},\qquad S_{\mathrm{cls}}(G_{m})=\sum_{c_{i}\in G_{m}}S_{\mathrm{ind}}(c_{i}). (8)

Based on the cluster-level and individual-level scores, we first select the most reliable cluster G∗=arg⁡maxGm∈𝒢​Scls​(Gm)G^{*}=\arg\max_{G_{m}\in\mathcal{G}}S_{\mathrm{cls}}(G_{m}), and then choose the most reliable code c∗c^{*} within it: c∗=arg⁡maxci∈G∗​Sind​(ci)c^{*}=\arg\max_{c_{i}\in G^{*}}S_{\mathrm{ind}}(c_{i}). When all executions are error-free, every within-cluster pair agrees on all RR inputs, yielding Scls​(Gm)=|Gm|​(|Gm|−1)​RS_{\mathrm{cls}}(G_{m})=|G_{m}|(|G_{m}|-1)R. Thus, with fixed RR, maximizing SclsS_{\mathrm{cls}} is equivalent to selecting the largest cluster. With runtime errors, the same score remains more reliable than raw cluster size because it rewards only ordered valid pairwise agreements.

3 Experiments

3.1 Settings

Datasets. For evaluation, we adopt the coding benchmarks suite curated by CURE [35], which includes four widely used and challenging datasets: LiveBench [37], LiveCodeBench (v2) [12], CodeContests [18], and CodeForces [25]. These datasets contain 128, 511, 239, and 467 problems, respectively. Detailed information can be viewed in Appendix G. To reduce computational cost, all experiments other than the main full-benchmark results in Table 1 are conducted on a 200-problem benchmark. For each random seed, we sample 50 problems from each dataset, resulting in 200 problems in total. We use three different random seeds to construct three independent 200-benchmarks and report the averaged results across them. Unless otherwise specified, all results beyond Table 1 are based on this 200-benchmark setting.

Baselines. We use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct [1] as the standard base models for CoSPlay and other TTS baselines: S* [16], SFS [19], MPSC [9], CodeTree [17], ThinkCoder [45] and PowerSampling [13]. We further benchmark against strong instruct and RLVR-trained models at 14B and 7B scales. At the 14B scale, baselines include Qwen2.5-14B-Coder, Qwen2.5-14B-Coder-Instruct [10], Absolute-Zero-14B [47], and CURE-14B [35]. At the 7B scale, we include Qwen2.5-7B-Coder, Qwen2.5-7B-Coder-Instruct [10], Seed-Coder-8B-Instruct [27], AceCoder-7B-RM, AceCoder-7B-Rule [43], CURE-7B [35], and Absolute-Zero-Coder-7B [47]. More detailed baseline settings are provided in Appendix 4.

Implementation Details All experiments are conducted on two NVIDIA H100 (80GB) GPUs using vLLM [14], with a temperature of 0.8, top-p of 0.95 and top-k of 40. In all experiments, we initialize half of the UT inputs using random valid inputs and the other half using inputs from 𝒜\mathcal{A}. For each generated UT input, we sample 4 expected outputs and keep the UT only if at least 3 outputs agree. Besides, for CoSPlay, we set the code pool size NcN_{c} to 16, the UT pool size NtN_{t} to 16, and the maximum iteration budget TmaxT_{\max} to 5.

3.2 Results

CoSPlay substantially improves both UT and code quality. Table 1 shows that CoSPlay consistently improves base models across most metrics without GT data or additional training. Starting from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, CoSPlay w/ Cluster improves average Signal, UT accuracy, code accuracy, and BoN from 22.1%, 14.6%, 19.0%, and 22.1% to 31.9%, 78.3%, 23.3%, and 33.2%, respectively. It slightly surpasses CURE-7B in average BoN (33.2% vs. 32.9%) while achieving much higher UT accuracy (78.3% vs. 54.9%). Similar trends hold at the 14B scale. When applied to CURE, CoSPlay further improves BoN from 32.9% to 38.6% on CURE-7B and from 41.8% to 46.2% on CURE-14B, demonstrating complementarity with RLVR. The consistent gains from the w/ Cluster rows further show that execution consensus provides more useful selection beyond BoN. Compared with CodeT [4], which also relies on execution-output agreement for selection, our Cluster-only variant achieves comparable performance, while both are outperformed by the full CoSPlay framework.

CoSPlay surpasses scaled TTS baselines. Figure 5(a) compares CoSPlay with TTS methods under their largest scaled configurations. CoSPlay forms the outer envelope of the radar plot on most axes, achieving higher Pass@1 across both 7B and 14B models on most benchmarks. Moreover, CoSPlay w/ Cluster further expands this envelope, showing that execution consensus can better select BoN-tied codes.One exception is Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct on LiveBench, where scaling BoN to N=256N=256 surpasses CoSPlay-14B, suggesting that simple sampling can still work well on easier benchmarks; however, this scaling alone is insufficient on harder benchmarks. These results indicate that allocating test-time compute to execution-guided verification, code refinement, and selection for Code-UT co-evolution is useful. Detailed results are reported in Table 5.

Ablation Study. Figure 5(b) shows that the full CoSPlay framework achieves the best BoN accuracy by the final self-play round. The w/o exp-atk variant consistently performs worst, confirming the importance of idea-level exploration for constructing a strong initial Code-UT pool. Removing individual self-play components, including Step 2, Step 3, the non-trivial-best heuristic, or self-consistency, also degrades performance, indicating that each module contributes to stable long-term improvement. Figure 5(c) further shows that the Signal of the full model increases consistently across rounds, suggesting that self-play progressively strengthens the discriminative power of the UT pool. In contrast, ablated variants exhibit weaker or unstable trajectories, especially w/o exp-atk, whose Signal declines over time. Detailed results are provided in Appendix H.

4 Discussion

4.1 Generalizability of CoSPlay

Generalization across model families. We evaluate CoSPlay on instruct, RLVR-tuned, and frontier-scale models to test the generalization. As shown in Figure 6(a), CoSPlay w/ Cluster improves the average BoN over the simple Best-of-16 baseline from 37.8% to 45.3%, yielding a +7.5% absolute gain. Table 6 in Appendix F further shows that these BoN gains come from jointly improving both code and UT accuracy across backbones. The gains are large across various instruct and RLVR-tuned models: Seed-Coder-8B-Instruct improves from 32.3% to 42.3%, DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite-Instruct-16B from 30.8% to 41.3%, AceCoder-Rule-7B from 29.0% to 39.5%, and AceCoder-RM-7B from 29.3% to 40.5%. These results suggest that CoSPlay is not specialized to one model family, scale, or post-training recipe, but can serve as a general inference-time complement to different backbones. We further evaluate CoSPlay on frontier-scale models. CoSPlay w/ Cluster raises the average BoN of DeepSeek-V3.2-685B from 65.7% to 68.2% and Gemini-2.0-Flash from 53.8% to 55.3%. The gains are more pronounced on CodeForces, the hardest benchmark in our suite, where CoSPlay w/ Cluster improves DeepSeek-V3.2-685B from 39.3% to 50.0% and Gemini-2.0-Flash from 36.7% to 38.7%. This suggests that CoSPlay still mines test-time gains from frontier-scale models, especially facing challenging problems.

When does self-play help? The gains are not uniform across different models and benchmarks, as shown in Table 6. This is tied to how CoSPlay obtains verification signal: both code quality and UT reliability are inferred from the backbone’s own generated Code-UT executions rather than GT. This signal become useful for self-play only when their pass-count statistics can distinguish higher-quality objects from lower-quality ones. This happens when support is aligned with correctness: correct codes tend to pass more generated UTs than incorrect codes, and reliable UTs tend to be passed by more candidate codes than unreliable UTs. When this alignment holds, row and column pass counts provide GT-free internal signals for ranking, refreshing, and repairing the Code-UT pool; the empirical correlation is shown in Figure 7, and the posterior direction is formalized in Appendix A.1.2. This gives a three-regime view of self-play. At the lower boundary, if the backbone is too weak for a benchmark, the initial UT correctness prior can fall below the code-side threshold ρT⋆\rho_{T}^{\star} analyzed in Appendix A.1.1. In this regime, passing more generated UTs no longer reliably indicates a more correct code candidate, so noisy or wrong-oracle tests and spurious Code-UT coupling can dominate the execution matrix and prevent stable improvement. At the upper boundary, if the backbone is already very strong, the Code-UT pool can approach saturation: low-support items selected for refresh may have similar expected quality to newly sampled or repaired items. Refreshing then provides little expected improvement and mainly introduces sampling variance, which can lead to fluctuations rather than monotonic gains. Between them, the backbone is strong enough for pass counts to remain correctness-aligned, while the current pool still contains low-support samples whose expected quality can be improved through regeneration or repair. Here, pass-count-guided updates can improve these weak samples and move the pool toward a more reliable state for final selection.

4.2 Exploration-Attack Guided Idea Generation Improves Initial UT Quality

Our exploration-attack (exp-atk) stage improves the accuracy and discriminativeness of initial UTs. As shown in Table 7 in Appendix H, even without self-play or self-consistency, exploration alone raises U​TAccUT_{\text{Acc}} from 12.5% to 37.2% and Signal from 26.5% to 33.7%. Figure 6(b) further explains this improvement from the pass-count distribution. Without exp-atk, most UTs concentrate near zero pass count, suggesting that many initial UTs are invalid, overly difficult, or tied to spurious code behavior. With exp-atk, the distribution shifts toward higher pass counts, increasing the average UT pass count by δ=2.39\delta=2.39 and reducing extreme low-support UTs by 29.0%. This indicates that exp-atk produces more reliable UTs that are supported by multiple candidate codes, while still preserving enough variation for selection. Together, these results show that exp-atk improves both UT correctness and discriminative power.

4.3 Pass Count Reflects True Accuracy

To validate that pass count reflects actual quality, we study the relationship between pass count and GT correctness for both code and UTs. As shown in Figure 7(e-f), both UTs and codes exhibit a strong positive correlation: UTs passed by more codes are more likely to be correct, while codes passing more UTs are also more likely to be functionally correct. Consistently, Figure 7(b-c) shows that correct candidates concentrate more heavily in high pass-count regions than wrong candidates. These results indicate that pass counts from the execution matrix can serve as an effective GT-free proxy for candidate quality.

4.4 Cluster-Based Selection Reflects Functional Consistency

Our cluster-based selection is built on the assumption that larger execution-consensus clusters are more likely to contain correct code. We first verify that cluster size is positively correlated with true code correctness. Figure 7(a) shows that correct codes concentrate in large clusters, while wrong codes mostly form clusters of size 1 or 2; Figure 7(d) further shows that average true code accuracy increases steadily with cluster size for both 7B and 14B models. This supports the intuition that correct codes tend to share consistent functional behavior, whereas wrong codes fail in diverse ways. We further verify that cluster size is positively correlated with our aggregate cluster score. As shown in Figure 6(c), larger clusters generally obtain higher scores for both CoSPlay-7B and CoSPlay-14B, indicating that our scoring rule preserves the largest-cluster intuition while adapting it to runtime-error settings. Since raw cluster size can be unreliable when candidates produce invalid executions, the cluster score aggregates valid pairwise agreements and provides a more robust estimate of cluster reliability.

4.5 Self-play progressively shifts pass-count distributions to the right

Figure 8 shows the average evolution of UT and code pass-count distributions from round 0 to round 5. For both 7B and 14B models, self-play consistently reduces the density in low pass-count regions and increases the density near the maximum pass count. This trend appears for both UTs and codes: fewer UTs remain rarely passed by the code pool, and more code candidates pass a larger number of UTs after iterative refinement. Quantitatively, the low-pass-density regions decrease by 29.9%/27.3% for UTs and 25.2%/23.3% for codes at the 7B/14B scales, while the high-pass-density regions increase accordingly. These results suggest that execution-matrix-driven self-play progressively removes low-support UTs and codes, improving UT reliability and code quality.

4.6 t-SNE Visualization of Clusters

Figure 9 provides t-SNE visualizations of code candidates from CoSPlay-7B and CoSPlay-14B using their execution-output similarity. By projecting output-similarity patterns into a low-dimensional space, we observe that correct codes (blue dots) tend to concentrate in large execution-consensus clusters, often including the largest cluster indicated by dashed blue circles. This observation is consistent with the intuition behind our strategy: functionally equivalent correct codes yield identical outputs for the same input, thereby exhibiting high consistency. In contrast, many incorrect codes (red dots) appear more scattered or form smaller isolated clusters, suggesting that their failure modes are often less consistent across random inputs. Together with the quantitative cluster-size analysis, this visualization provides qualitative evidence that cluster size can serve as a useful empirical proxy for code correctness. Larger clusters generally indicate stronger output consistency and are empirically associated with a higher likelihood of correctness. This provides additional support for using output-consensus clustering to select more functionally consistent candidates from the code pool.

4.7 Scalability of CoSPlay with Increasing Candidate-Pool Size

As shown in Figure (a), both Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and CURE-7B obtain higher BoN as kk increases with CoSPlay, indicating that our method can effectively exploit larger inference-time candidate pools. Notably, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct + CoSPlay becomes comparable to CURE-7B when k≥16k\geq 16, despite using no GT data or training. At k=64k=64, CoSPlay improves Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct by 13.2%, while CURE-7B + CoSPlay continues to benefit from larger budgets, showing that CoSPlay can further enhance already RLVR-tuned models. Moreover, both CoSPlay settings show no clear saturation at k=64k=64, suggesting that performance may continue to improve with larger candidate pools; however, we leave this further scaling study to future work due to computational resource constraints.

4.8 UT Accuracy-Diversity Trade-off of CoSPlay

To quantify UT diversity, we define the UT rank 𝒯rank=|{xj∣(xj,yj)∈𝒯}|\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{rank}}=\left|\{x_{j}\mid(x_{j},y_{j})\in\mathcal{T}\}\right| as the number of unique test inputs in the pool 𝒯\mathcal{T}. While this metric does not fully capture semantic diversity, it provides a lightweight estimate of UT diversity. Figure (b) shows that CoSPlay-enhanced models achieve a better UT accuracy-diversity trade-off than the original baselines. Without CoSPlay, the Pareto frontier is mainly formed by models that favor either high diversity with low accuracy or high accuracy with low diversity. After applying CoSPlay, the corresponding points move closer to the upper-right region, indicating improved balance between UT correctness and diversity. CURE-14B is a representative case: it achieves high UT accuracy but relatively low UT rank, suggesting that RL-based training may improve correctness while reducing diversity [48]. CoSPlay alleviates this issue by promoting UT diversity through idea-level exploration, while preserving UT accuracy by filtering low-quality UTs with pass-count signals from the execution matrix. Qwen-based models and CURE-7B mainly gain in UT accuracy with slightly decreased yet competitive rank. The larger marker sizes further indicate higher BoN and Signal scores, showing that this improved trade-off translates into stronger final selection capability.

4.9 Efficiency Analysis of CoSPlay

Figure  compares CoSPlay with TTS methods under different token budgets. Although full CoSPlay uses additional computation for Code-UT generation, execution, and self-play, existing TTS baselines still achieve lower Pass@1 when scaled to comparable or even larger token costs. Moreover, as the inference budget increases, CoSPlay improves faster than competing TTS baselines, indicating stronger budget scalability rather than a simple constant gain. This shows that CoSPlay attains a higher performance ceiling rather than merely benefiting from larger inference budgets. The ablation variants further show that even after removing costly components such as self-consistency and UT iteration, CoSPlay substantially reduces token consumption while still outperforming most baselines, and in some cases even surpasses baselines scaled to much larger budgets. These results suggest that CoSPlay provides a favorable cost-performance trade-off by allocating test-time compute to verifiable Code-UT co-evolution rather than undirected candidate sampling.

5 Conclusion and Future Directions

We introduce CoSPlay, a GT-free and training-free test-time scaling framework that jointly optimizes code candidates and unit tests via execution-driven co-evolution. CoSPlay first explores diverse high-level solution strategies together with their potential failure modes to derive discriminative UT ideas for better UT generation. It then leverages execution-matrix pass-count signals to iteratively refine both the code pool and the UT pool through cooperative self-play. Finally, for BoN-tied codes, CoSPlay further performs output-consensus clustering on random valid inputs. Since correct codes tend to produce consistent outputs while incorrect ones often diverge in different ways, it first selects the most reliable consensus cluster and then chooses the highest-reliability code within that cluster as the final solution. It consistently outperforms GT-free TTS baselines and matches or surpasses RLVR methods, improving both UT and code quality. These results suggest a scalable route toward GT-free test-time improvement for verifiable reasoning.

Limitation and Future Directions. CoSPlay relies on an executable environment to obtain Code-UT feedback, making direct extension to non-executable reasoning tasks more challenging. CoSPlay also consumes more tokens due to iterative Code-UT evolution. However, under comparable test-time compute budgets, it achieves the best performance among evaluated methods and substantially outperforms existing GT-free TTS methods. Improving token efficiency and extending to broader reasoning tasks remain promising directions.

Appendix

Appendix A Theory Analysis

A.1 Analysis of Pass-Count Signals

This section analyzes an i.i.d. model for the standard BoN baseline where codes and UTs are sampled independently. The goal is to explain why pass counts can serve as statistical signals for both code quality and UT quality. The first part introduces the execution-matrix setup and the thresholds under which pass counts allow codes and UTs to judge each other’s reliability. The second part derives the posterior direction and convergence rate induced by binomial support counts.

A.1.1 When Pass Counts Indicate Correctness

Consider one independent sampling round under the standard BoN baseline: code candidates and a UT pool are generated without self-play updates. Fix a coding problem, and let

𝒞={ci}i=1Nc,𝒯={tj}j=1Nt,tj=(xj,yj).\mathcal{C}=\{c_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N_{c}},\qquad\mathcal{T}=\{t_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N_{t}},\qquad t_{j}=(x_{j},y_{j}).

The execution matrix are

Mi​j:=𝟏{Exec(ci,xj)=yj},M_{ij}:=\mathbf{1}\{\operatorname{Exec}(c_{i},x_{j})=y_{j}\},

the UT-side and code-side pass counts, and their corresponding pass rates represented as:

pjUT=∑i=1NcMi​j,picode=∑j=1NtMi​j,αjUT=pjUTNc,αicode=picodeNt.p_{j}^{\mathrm{UT}}=\sum_{i=1}^{N_{c}}M_{ij},\qquad p_{i}^{\mathrm{code}}=\sum_{j=1}^{N_{t}}M_{ij},\qquad\alpha_{j}^{\mathrm{UT}}=\frac{p_{j}^{\mathrm{UT}}}{N_{c}},\qquad\alpha_{i}^{\mathrm{code}}=\frac{p_{i}^{\mathrm{code}}}{N_{t}}.

Here pjUTp_{j}^{\mathrm{UT}} and αjUT\alpha_{j}^{\mathrm{UT}} are UT-side support statistics, while picodep_{i}^{\mathrm{code}} and αicode\alpha_{i}^{\mathrm{code}} are code-side support statistics. Runtime errors are treated as failures.

Let C+C^{+} and U+U^{+} denote the events that a randomly sampled code and a randomly sampled test are correct, respectively. Let C−C^{-} and U−U^{-} denote their complements, and write

ρC=ℙ⁡(C+),ρT=ℙ⁡(U+),0<ρC,ρT<1.\rho_{C}=\mathbb{P}(C^{+}),\qquad\rho_{T}=\mathbb{P}(U^{+}),\qquad 0<\rho_{C},\rho_{T}<1.

Codes and tests are sampled independently. After conditioning on the correctness state of the evaluated object, pass events from different evaluators are conditionally independent. A correct code always passes a correct test and always fails an incorrect test; the only randomness comes from incorrect codes. Let ε1,ε2∈[0,1]\varepsilon_{1},\varepsilon_{2}\in[0,1] be the pass rates of an incorrect code on a correct test and on an incorrect test, respectively:

ℙ⁡(M=1∣C+,U+)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(M=1\mid C^{+},U^{+}) =1,\displaystyle=1,\qquad ℙ⁡(M=1∣C+,U−)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(M=1\mid C^{+},U^{-}) =0,\displaystyle=0,
ℙ⁡(M=1∣C−,U+)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(M=1\mid C^{-},U^{+}) =ε1,\displaystyle=\varepsilon_{1}, ℙ⁡(M=1∣C−,U−)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(M=1\mid C^{-},U^{-}) =ε2.\displaystyle=\varepsilon_{2}.

By the law of total probability and independence, the marginal pass probabilities are

θ1\displaystyle\theta_{1} :=ℙ⁡(M=1∣U+)=ρC+(1−ρC)​ε1,\displaystyle:=\mathbb{P}(M=1\mid U^{+})=\rho_{C}+(1-\rho_{C})\varepsilon_{1}, (9)
θ0\displaystyle\theta_{0} :=ℙ⁡(M=1∣U−)=(1−ρC)​ε2,\displaystyle:=\mathbb{P}(M=1\mid U^{-})=(1-\rho_{C})\varepsilon_{2},
φ1\displaystyle\varphi_{1} :=ℙ⁡(M=1∣C+)=ρT,\displaystyle:=\mathbb{P}(M=1\mid C^{+})=\rho_{T},
φ0\displaystyle\varphi_{0} :=ℙ⁡(M=1∣C−)=ε1​ρT+ε2​(1−ρT).\displaystyle:=\mathbb{P}(M=1\mid C^{-})=\varepsilon_{1}\rho_{T}+\varepsilon_{2}(1-\rho_{T}).

θ1,θ0\theta_{1},\theta_{0} are the probabilities that a correct or incorrect test is passed by a random code. φ1,φ0\varphi_{1},\varphi_{0} are the probabilities that a correct or incorrect code passes a random test. The former captures the fact that correct tests should be easier to pass, while incorrect tests should be harder to pass. The latter captures the fact that correct codes should pass tests more often, whereas the pass noise of incorrect codes is controlled by ε1\varepsilon_{1} and ε2\varepsilon_{2}. The gaps between the positive and negative classes quantify the attraction advantage of positive objects over negative objects on an execution-matrix entry MM:

ΔU\displaystyle\Delta_{U} :=θ1−θ0=ρC+(1−ρC)​(ε1−ε2),\displaystyle:=\theta_{1}-\theta_{0}=\rho_{C}+(1-\rho_{C})(\varepsilon_{1}-\varepsilon_{2}), ΔU>0\displaystyle\Delta_{U}>0 ⟺ρC>ρC⋆:=ε2−ε11+ε2−ε1,\displaystyle\Longleftrightarrow\rho_{C}>\rho_{C}^{\star}:=\frac{\varepsilon_{2}-\varepsilon_{1}}{1+\varepsilon_{2}-\varepsilon_{1}}, (10)
ΔC\displaystyle\Delta_{C} :=φ1−φ0=ρT​(1−ε1)−ε2​(1−ρT),\displaystyle:=\varphi_{1}-\varphi_{0}=\rho_{T}(1-\varepsilon_{1})-\varepsilon_{2}(1-\rho_{T}), ΔC>0\displaystyle\Delta_{C}>0 ⟺ρT>ρT⋆:=ε21−ε1+ε2.\displaystyle\Longleftrightarrow\rho_{T}>\rho_{T}^{\star}:=\frac{\varepsilon_{2}}{1-\varepsilon_{1}+\varepsilon_{2}}.

The UT-side advantage ΔU\Delta_{U} is easier to obtain. Any correct code passes correct UTs, and partially correct code can still pass UTs that match its correct logic. In contrast, wrong code can pass a wrong-output UT only when it matches that specific wrong logic. Since correct solutions share the same answer logic while wrong answers are usually dispersed, a usable base model is unlikely to make wrong code pass wrong-output UTs more often than correct UTs, namely ε1≥ε2\varepsilon_{1}\geq\varepsilon_{2}. This makes the UT-side threshold easy to satisfy. The code-side advantage ΔC\Delta_{C} is also controlled by the incorrect-test noise ε2\varepsilon_{2}. When both ε1\varepsilon_{1} and ε2\varepsilon_{2} are small, ρT⋆\rho_{T}^{\star} is also small. However, the code side still requires the fraction of correct tests ρT\rho_{T} in the UT pool to exceed this noise level ρT⋆\rho_{T}^{\star}. Hence its threshold is relatively higher than the UT-side threshold, and it needs a sufficiently high probability of correctness to keep discriminative.

A.1.2 Support-Count Posterior

Each object to be judged is evaluated by mm sources. The ii-th source returns a binary support result Xi∈{0,1}X_{i}\in\{0,1\}, and the support count is S=∑i=1mXiS=\sum_{i=1}^{m}X_{i}. If these results are independent and identically distributed under each hypothesis, then SS follows the corresponding binomial distribution. In the notation of the main CoSPlay paper, the UT side takes m=Ncm=N_{c} and S=pjUTS=p_{j}^{\mathrm{UT}}, while the code side takes m=Ntm=N_{t} and §=picode\lx@sectionsign=p_{i}^{\mathrm{code}}.

Theorem A.1 (Posterior direction of support counts).

Suppose the support count SS satisfies

S∣H+∼Binomial(m,q1),S∣H−∼Binomial(m,q0),S\mid H^{+}\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(m,q_{1}),\qquad S\mid H^{-}\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(m,q_{0}),

where H+H^{+} is the hypothesis that the object is correct, H−H^{-} is the hypothesis that the object is incorrect, q1q_{1} is the probability that a correct object is supported by one evaluator, q0q_{0} is the probability that an incorrect object is supported by one evaluator, and 0<q0,q1<10<q_{0},q_{1}<1. If q1>q0q_{1}>q_{0}, then a larger support count implies a larger posterior probability of correctness. If q1=q0q_{1}=q_{0}, the support count does not change the posterior. If q1<q0q_{1}<q_{0}, then a larger support count implies a smaller posterior probability of correctness. The posterior odds ratio changes exponentially with the support count.

Proof.

Let the prior be ρ=ℙ⁡(H+)∈(0,1)\rho=\mathbb{P}(H^{+})\in(0,1). By Bayes’ rule and the binomial probability mass function,

OR⁡(s)\displaystyle\operatorname{OR}(s) :=ℙ⁡(H+∣S=s)ℙ⁡(H−∣S=s)=ρ1−ρ(ms)​q1s​(1−q1)m−s(ms)​q0s​(1−q0)m−s=ρ1−ρ(1−q11−q0)mrs,r:=q1​(1−q0)q0​(1−q1).\displaystyle:=\frac{\mathbb{P}(H^{+}\mid S=s)}{\mathbb{P}(H^{-}\mid S=s)}=\frac{\rho}{1-\rho}\frac{\binom{m}{s}q_{1}^{s}(1-q_{1})^{m-s}}{\binom{m}{s}q_{0}^{s}(1-q_{0})^{m-s}}=\frac{\rho}{1-\rho}\left(\frac{1-q_{1}}{1-q_{0}}\right)^{m}r^{s},r:=\frac{q_{1}(1-q_{0})}{q_{0}(1-q_{1})}. (11)

The posterior probability and the odds ratio satisfy

ℙ⁡(H+∣S=s)=OR⁡(s)1+OR⁡(s).\mathbb{P}(H^{+}\mid S=s)=\frac{\operatorname{OR}(s)}{1+\operatorname{OR}(s)}. (12)

The function x↦x/(1+x)x\mapsto x/(1+x) is strictly increasing on x>0x>0, and

r>1⟺q1​(1−q0)>q0​(1−q1)⟺q1>q0.r>1\Longleftrightarrow q_{1}(1-q_{0})>q_{0}(1-q_{1})\Longleftrightarrow q_{1}>q_{0}.

Thus the sign of q1−q0q_{1}-q_{0} determines the posterior direction:

  1. 1.

    If q1>q0q_{1}>q_{0}, then r>1r>1. Both the posterior odds ratio and the posterior probability of correctness are strictly increasing in ss.

  2. 2.

    If q1=q0q_{1}=q_{0}, then r=1r=1. The support count changes neither the posterior odds ratio nor the posterior probability of correctness.

  3. 3.

    If q1<q0q_{1}<q_{0}, then 0<r<10<r<1. Both the posterior odds ratio and the posterior probability of correctness are strictly decreasing in ss.

Moreover, Eq. (11) shows that the posterior odds ratio depends on ss through the exponential factor rsr^{s}. ∎

Corollary A.2 (Posterior convergence at a fixed support ratio).

Under the binomial model in Theorem A.1, let mm be the number of independent evaluators, and let s=⌊η​m⌋s=\lfloor\eta m\rfloor, where η∈[0,1]\eta\in[0,1] is fixed. If q1≠q0q_{1}\neq q_{0}, then there exists a unique threshold η⋆\eta^{\star} between q0q_{0} and q1q_{1}. As m→∞m\to\infty, any fixed support ratio on the side biased toward q1q_{1} makes the posterior probability of correctness converge exponentially fast to 11, while any fixed support ratio on the other side makes it converge exponentially fast to 00. If q1=q0q_{1}=q_{0} or η=η⋆\eta=\eta^{\star}, no exponential decision is obtained.

Proof.

Let the prior be ρ=ℙ⁡(H+)∈(0,1)\rho=\mathbb{P}(H^{+})\in(0,1), and write

r:=q1​(1−q0)q0​(1−q1).r:=\frac{q_{1}(1-q_{0})}{q_{0}(1-q_{1})}.

Let δm=s−η​m\delta_{m}=s-\eta m. Since s=⌊η​m⌋s=\lfloor\eta m\rfloor, we have |δm|≤1|\delta_{m}|\leq 1. By Eq. (11),

log⁡OR⁡(s)\displaystyle\log\operatorname{OR}(s) =log⁡ρ1−ρ+m​log⁡1−q11−q0+s​log⁡r\displaystyle=\log\frac{\rho}{1-\rho}+m\log\frac{1-q_{1}}{1-q_{0}}+s\log r
=log⁡ρ1−ρ+m⁡[log⁡1−q11−q0+η​log⁡r]+δm​log⁡r\displaystyle=\log\frac{\rho}{1-\rho}+m\left[\log\frac{1-q_{1}}{1-q_{0}}+\eta\log r\right]+\delta_{m}\log r
=log⁡ρ1−ρ+m⁡[log⁡1−q11−q0+η​log⁡q1​(1−q0)q0​(1−q1)]+O⁡(1)\displaystyle=\log\frac{\rho}{1-\rho}+m\left[\log\frac{1-q_{1}}{1-q_{0}}+\eta\log\frac{q_{1}(1-q_{0})}{q_{0}(1-q_{1})}\right]+O(1)
=log⁡ρ1−ρ+m⁡[η​log⁡q1q0+(1−η)​log⁡1−q11−q0]+O⁡(1)\displaystyle=\log\frac{\rho}{1-\rho}+m\left[\eta\log\frac{q_{1}}{q_{0}}+(1-\eta)\log\frac{1-q_{1}}{1-q_{0}}\right]+O(1)
=log⁡ρ1−ρ+m​D​(η)+O⁡(1).\displaystyle=\log\frac{\rho}{1-\rho}+mD(\eta)+O(1).

Here

D⁡(η):=η​log⁡q1q0+(1−η)​log⁡1−q11−q0.D(\eta):=\eta\log\frac{q_{1}}{q_{0}}+(1-\eta)\log\frac{1-q_{1}}{1-q_{0}}. (13)

If q1=q0q_{1}=q_{0}, then D⁡(η)≡0D(\eta)\equiv 0. We now assume q1≠q0q_{1}\neq q_{0}. By Eq. (13),

D(q0)=−KL(Bern(q0)∥Bern(q1))<0,D(q1)=KL(Bern(q1)∥Bern(q0))>0.D(q_{0})=-\operatorname{KL}\big(\operatorname{Bern}(q_{0})\|\operatorname{Bern}(q_{1})\big)<0,\qquad D(q_{1})=\operatorname{KL}\big(\operatorname{Bern}(q_{1})\|\operatorname{Bern}(q_{0})\big)>0.

Thus DD is a nonconstant linear function, and its unique zero lies between q0q_{0} and q1q_{1}. Solving D⁡(η⋆)=0D(\eta^{\star})=0 in Eq. (13) gives

η⋆:=log⁡{(1−q0)/(1−q1)}log⁡r.\eta^{\star}:=\frac{\log\{(1-q_{0})/(1-q_{1})\}}{\log r}.

Finally, by Eq. (12),

ℙ⁡(H+∣S=s)=11+exp⁡{−log⁡OR⁡(s)}=11+exp⁡{−m​D​(η)+O⁡(1)}.\mathbb{P}(H^{+}\mid S=s)=\frac{1}{1+\exp\{-\log\operatorname{OR}(s)\}}=\frac{1}{1+\exp\{-mD(\eta)+O(1)\}}.

Moreover, D′​(η)=log⁡rD^{\prime}(\eta)=\log r. We distinguish three cases:

  1. 1.

    If q1>q0q_{1}>q_{0}, then DD is strictly increasing. Hence, when η>η⋆\eta>\eta^{\star}, D⁡(η)>0D(\eta)>0, and the posterior probability of correctness converges exponentially fast to 11. When η<η⋆\eta<\eta^{\star}, D⁡(η)<0D(\eta)<0, and the posterior probability of correctness converges exponentially fast to 00.

  2. 2.

    If q1<q0q_{1}<q_{0}, then DD is strictly decreasing, so the sign direction is reversed. Hence, when η<η⋆\eta<\eta^{\star}, the posterior probability of correctness converges exponentially fast to 11, and when η>η⋆\eta>\eta^{\star}, it converges exponentially fast to 00.

  3. 3.

A.2 Analysis of Execution-Consensus Clustering

Execution-Consensus Clustering is applied after BoN filtering. Let 𝒞high\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{high}} be the high-scoring set retained by BoN, and draw a code cc from this set. All probabilities below are conditional on c∈𝒞highc\in\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{high}} and are taken over both code and input randomness. Draw RR independent valid random inputs z1,…,zRz_{1},\ldots,z_{R}, and write

σ⁡(c):=(c⁡(z1),…,c⁡(zR)),σ+=(σ1+,…,σR+),\sigma(c):=\big(c(z_{1}),\ldots,c(z_{R})\big),\qquad\sigma^{+}=(\sigma^{+}_{1},\ldots,\sigma^{+}_{R}),

where 𝝈⁡(c)\boldsymbol{\sigma}(c) is the output signature of candidate cc, and σ+\sigma^{+} is the correct output signature.

Proposition A.3 (Separation of the correct output signature).

Suppose α:=ℙ⁡(C+)>0\alpha:=\mathbb{P}(C^{+})>0, and there exists β∈[0,1)\beta\in[0,1) such that every incorrect code cc, output value yy, and r∈[1,R]r\in[1,R] satisfy ℙ⁡(c⁡(zr)=y∣c)≤β\mathbb{P}(c(z_{r})=y\mid c)\leq\beta. Then, for sufficiently large RR, σ+\sigma^{+} is the unique maximum-probability signature. Moreover, for any such RR, if the signature space is finite and candidates are sampled independently, then the largest empirical cluster converges almost surely to the correct output-consensus cluster.

Proof.

A correct code has output signature σ+\sigma^{+}, so ℙ⁡(σ⁡(c)=σ+∣C+)=1\mathbb{P}(\sigma(c)=\sigma^{+}\mid C^{+})=1. By the law of total probability,

ℙ⁡(σ⁡(c)=σ+)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\big(\sigma(c)=\sigma^{+}\big) =ℙ⁡(C+)​ℙ​(σ⁡(c)=σ+∣C+)+ℙ⁡(C−)​ℙ​(σ⁡(c)=σ+∣C−)\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}(C^{+})\mathbb{P}\big(\sigma(c)=\sigma^{+}\mid C^{+}\big)+\mathbb{P}(C^{-})\mathbb{P}\big(\sigma(c)=\sigma^{+}\mid C^{-}\big) (14)
≥ℙ⁡(C+)​ℙ​(σ⁡(c)=σ+∣C+)=α.\displaystyle\geq\mathbb{P}(C^{+})\mathbb{P}\big(\sigma(c)=\sigma^{+}\mid C^{+}\big)=\alpha.

Let 𝒮R\mathcal{S}_{R} be the length-RR output-signature space, write 𝒮R−:=𝒮R∖{σ+}\mathcal{S}_{R}^{-}:=\mathcal{S}_{R}\setminus\{\sigma^{+}\}, and take any incorrect signature σ−=(σ1−,…,σR−)∈𝒮R−\sigma^{-}=(\sigma^{-}_{1},\ldots,\sigma^{-}_{R})\in\mathcal{S}_{R}^{-}. A correct code never produces an incorrect signature, so

ℙ⁡(σ⁡(c)=σ−∣C+)=0.\mathbb{P}\big(\sigma(c)=\sigma^{-}\mid C^{+}\big)=0.

The anti-concentration condition and the independence of z1,…,zRz_{1},\ldots,z_{R} give

ℙ⁡(σ⁡(c)=σ−∣C−)=𝔼c|C−​[ℙ⁡(σ⁡(c)=σ−∣c)]=𝔼c|C−​[∏r=1Rℙ⁡(c⁡(zr)=σr−∣c)]≤βR.\mathbb{P}\big(\sigma(c)=\sigma^{-}\mid C^{-}\big)=\mathbb{E}_{c\mid C^{-}}\left[\mathbb{P}\big(\sigma(c)=\sigma^{-}\mid c\big)\right]=\mathbb{E}_{c\mid C^{-}}\left[\prod_{r=1}^{R}\mathbb{P}\big(c(z_{r})=\sigma^{-}_{r}\mid c\big)\right]\leq\beta^{R}.

Again by the law of total probability,

ℙ⁡(σ⁡(c)=σ−)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\big(\sigma(c)=\sigma^{-}\big) =ℙ⁡(C+)​ℙ​(σ⁡(c)=σ−∣C+)+ℙ⁡(C−)​ℙ​(σ⁡(c)=σ−∣C−)\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}(C^{+})\mathbb{P}\big(\sigma(c)=\sigma^{-}\mid C^{+}\big)+\mathbb{P}(C^{-})\mathbb{P}\big(\sigma(c)=\sigma^{-}\mid C^{-}\big) (15)
=(1−α)​ℙ​(σ⁡(c)=σ−∣C−)≤(1−α)​βR.\displaystyle=(1-\alpha)\mathbb{P}\big(\sigma(c)=\sigma^{-}\mid C^{-}\big)\leq(1-\alpha)\beta^{R}.

Combining Eqs. (14) and (15), and taking the supremum over incorrect signatures, gives

ℙ⁡(σ⁡(c)=σ+)−supσ−∈𝒮R−ℙ⁡(σ⁡(c)=σ−)≥α−(1−α)​βR→R→∞α>0.\mathbb{P}\big(\sigma(c)=\sigma^{+}\big)-\sup_{\sigma^{-}\in\mathcal{S}_{R}^{-}}\mathbb{P}\big(\sigma(c)=\sigma^{-}\big)\geq\alpha-(1-\alpha)\beta^{R}\xrightarrow{R\to\infty}\alpha>0.

Therefore, for sufficiently large RR, σ+\sigma^{+} has strictly larger probability than any incorrect signature and is the unique population mode.

Take such an RR, and let δR:=ℙ⁡(σ⁡(c)=σ+)−supσ−∈𝒮R−ℙ⁡(σ⁡(c)=σ−)>0\delta_{R}:=\mathbb{P}(\sigma(c)=\sigma^{+})-\sup_{\sigma^{-}\in\mathcal{S}_{R}^{-}}\mathbb{P}(\sigma(c)=\sigma^{-})>0. If candidates c1,…,cnc_{1},\ldots,c_{n} are sampled independently from 𝒞high\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{high}}, then for any incorrect signature σ−\sigma^{-}, the strong law of large numbers gives

1n∑i=1n(𝟏{σ(ci)=σ+}−𝟏{σ(ci)=σ−})→a.s.ℙ(σ(c)=σ+)−ℙ(σ(c)=σ−)≥δR.\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\mathbf{1}\{\sigma(c_{i})=\sigma^{+}\}-\mathbf{1}\{\sigma(c_{i})=\sigma^{-}\}\right)\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}\mathbb{P}\big(\sigma(c)=\sigma^{+}\big)-\mathbb{P}\big(\sigma(c)=\sigma^{-}\big)\geq\delta_{R}.

Since 𝒮R\mathcal{S}_{R} is finite, this convergence holds for all incorrect signatures simultaneously. Hence, almost surely, there exists n0n_{0} such that for every n≥n0n\geq n_{0}, the empirical cluster size of σ+\sigma^{+} is strictly larger than that of every incorrect signature. Therefore the largest empirical cluster is eventually the correct output-consensus cluster. ∎

Appendix B Detailed Algorithm Design

Appendix C Related Work

C.1 Fine-tuning Methods for Code Generation

For code generation, most existing training-based methods rely heavily on external ground-truth data, approaches like μ\muCode [11] and AceCoder [43] employ Supervised Fine-Tuning using ground-truth or synthetic datasets, while Focused DPO [44] and CTRL [38] utilize RLVR by optimizing rewards design. Similarly, O1-Coder [46] and UTGen [26] fine-tune models specifically for UT generation by leveraging ground-truth code. Some recent approaches aim to co-evolve these capabilities using RLVR but often retain critical dependencies: UTRL [15] requires ground-truth code, and CURE [35] relies on ground-truth UT. While Absolute-Zero [47] achieves purely self-supervised learning without external data, it demands prohibitive computational resources for RLVR training.

C.2 TTS for LLM Code Generation

Test-Time Scaling (TTS) strategies typically begin with repeated sampling, such as Best-of-N (BoN), but they often struggle to identify the best candidate without GT data. To improve selection, consensus-based methods such as CodeT [4] and MPSC [9] use self-generated UTs for voting, although CodeT is limited by the potential unreliability of generated tests and MPSC incurs substantial overhead from extensive sampling. More broadly, sampling-based inference-time methods such as PowerSampling improve reasoning by drawing from sharpened sequence-level distributions without additional training, suggesting that stronger performance can sometimes be elicited purely through better test-time sampling [13]. Beyond simple resampling, a growing line of work treats code generation as a structured search problem. SFS formulates code generation as black-box optimization in code space and improves exploration diversity to avoid local optima [19], while CodeTree organizes planning, generation, and debugging within a unified tree structure guided by both execution feedback and agent feedback [17]. ThinkCoder further decomposes test-time computation into a thorough exploration stage followed by an optimal refinement stage, improving efficiency by first broadening the solution space and then sharpening promising candidates [45]. Finally, execution-guided approaches leverage runtime feedback for iterative improvement. Methods such as ORPS [41], S* [16], LDB [49], and Reflexion [28] use execution signals for process supervision or refinement. Another paper [5] further shows that self-generated tests can support iterative debugging, while also highlighting the bias and reliability issues that arise when such tests are used naively.

C.3 Self-Play in LLM

The self-play paradigm, popularized by AlphaZero  [30] and AlphaGo [29], has recently been adapted to optimize LLMs via RL. However, most existing approaches in the coding domain remain dependent on external supervision and heavy training. For instance, CURE  [35] relies on GT UT to guide the co-evolution of generation capability of code and UT, while UTRL  [15] necessitates ground-truth code for improving model performance. Although Absolute-Zero  [47] achieves a fully self-supervised setup without human data, it yields limited performance gains despite the prohibitive training costs of RLVR training. Crucially, these methods are exclusively training-time optimizations. In contrast, CoSPlay explores inference-time self-play for GT-free code generation, leveraging the pass count in execution metrix as signals to iteratively refine and filter candidates without parameter updates.

C.4 Search in Natural Language Space

To enhance the reasoning capabilities of LLMs, recent studies have proposed Chain-of-Thought [36] strategies into structured search processes within the natural language space. Frameworks such as Tree of Thoughts [39] and Reasoning via Planning [7] treat reasoning steps as a search tree, exploring various intermediate thoughts to reach a solution. In the specific domain of code generation, methods like PlanSearch [34] demonstrate that generating high-level natural language plans before implementation significantly outperforms direct code generation. The primary benefit of such natural language search lies in its ability to introduce structural diversity, preventing the model from converging to a narrow set of repetitive solutions—a common issue in direct code resampling. However, most existing methods for code generation remain static, generating plans without leveraging dynamic execution feedback or iterative self-play to refine.

Appendix D Detailed baseline setting

RL Baselines. Detailed data usage and base models are listed in Table 2. We follow the original prompts and LLM parameters as provided in each method’s code or paper.

TTS Baselines. For a fair comparison, we control the total code and UT generation budgets to be comparable across methods, and all UTs are generated by the model itself without external supervision. Specific settings are as follows:

(1) SFS [19]: num_seed = 10, max_iters = 40 (total budget of 50) and we scale to 80, generated UT = 6; we use the Role seed theme, the best-performing variant reported in the original paper. The sampling temperature is 0.20.2.

(2) CodeTree [17]: full agent setting with max budget = 50, generated UT = 6, max depth = 5, search width = 10. The scaled-up setting with max budget = 1000, generated UT = 16, max depth = 20, search width = 100. The sampling temperature is 0.00.0.

(3) MPSC [9]: solution = 60, specification = 50, test case = 100; we use MPSC-label mode, the best-performing mode for code generation reported in the original paper. The scaled-up setting with solution = 300, specification = 250, test case = 600. The sampling temperature is 0.80.8.

(4) PowerSampling [13]: n_samples = 16, mcmc_steps = 10, code sampling and UT generation temperature = 0.6.

(5) ThinkCoder [45]: k=20k=20 per iteration, each candidate prompted to generate 3 UTs, temperature is 1.0. budget nn to 2, and we scale to 5/10/20

(6) S* [16]: we use the local S* pipeline with generated UT = 16, N=16N=16 code samples per round, num_round=3\texttt{num\_round}=3 and we scale to 6. The sampling temperature is 0.70.7.

(7) BoN: we set N = 16/64/128/256 for both code and UT.
